correctness.rationale: With no rational base point, exactly one of the four members vanishes at each of the 13 rational points. A smooth blocking cubic cannot contain a rational line's four points and therefore has at least six points by the nontrivial prime-plane blocking bound; each smooth cubic has at least one point by Hasse–Weil. Thus two blocking members would require at least 14 points. An independent exact evaluation of all 29,524 normalized cubic equations found 4,940 blocking equations, including 936 smooth ones with six points each (234 supports), and matched their projective evaluation signatures exactly with the orbit of the stated F. Projective evaluation signatures are injective on cubic classes because a cubic vanishing at all 13 points would have all 13 line factors. Smoothness was tested over F₃, F₉ and F₂₇: an absolutely irreducible singular cubic has just one singular point, fixed by Frobenius; a line plus irreducible conic has an intersection point of degree at most two; three distinct lines give at most three singular intersections permuted by Frobenius; and a multiple line is unique and rational. Hence the finite test is exhaustive for this degree. Fixing G(P₀)=1 and its X³ coefficient to zero gives exactly one generator per eligible pencil through F. Of 6,561 candidates, 864 have no rational base point, 576 also have G smooth, and 312 have all four members smooth. Their local profile counts are (1,1,5):24, (1,2,4):132, (1,3,3):42, (2,2,3):114. The complete accepted coefficient set matches the frozen reference list, including the explicit witness with counts 6,4,1,2. Transitivity and uniqueness of the blocking member permit multiplication by 936 without double counting, which gives all the displayed global multiplicities.
residual_risks: The count concerns fixed-coordinate two-dimensional subspaces, with rational base points excluded; it is not a census up to isomorphism or a smoothness statement for non-rational parameters.

Kaplan–Matei give ordered cubic-pair counts by common rational points without all-four smoothness or blocking imposed.

The unrestricted pair count and the more relevant all-smooth census have broader populations, but their reported marginals do not record the distribution of the three other point counts within the blocking slice.

evidence: With a fixed F there are exactly three projective partners per pencil. With at most one blocking member, multiplying the prior orbit bin divided by three by 936 gives the global total without duplicate pencils.

The three other point counts must sum to seven and be positive. This allows exactly the four candidate partitions, but these constraints and the aggregate bin do not determine which occur or their frequencies.

The earlier pair algorithm could be modified to compute it, but its theorem and the inspected tallies do not imply it as an aggregate identity.

originality.rationale: The individual blocking orbit is prior coverage, and the earlier ambient all-smooth census already provides an orbit-by-rational-base-point tally whose blocking-orbit zero-base bin gives the per-cubic and global totals after dividing by three and weighting by orbit size. The supported distinct finding is the joint point-count spectrum within that bin. The earlier census and its inspected companion programs aggregate by base count, not by the rational point counts of the three other members. The four profile multiplicities are not determined by those aggregate outputs. Neither the previously known blocking orbit nor the earlier ambient tally is credited as new.
residual_risks: An uninspected per-pencil data dump or unindexed computation could encode the joint profiles. The available prior code and orbit/base aggregate outputs do not record them.
Availability of the ambient enumeration considerably reduces the work of independently computing this refinement; no broad priority claim is made.

value.rationale: This resolves a natural joint invariant for the first odd field admitting smooth blocking cubics: the point-count distribution of the three complements when an all-smooth basepoint-free pencil contains the blocking orbit. The distinction between the possible partitions of seven and their actual frequencies is genuine; the complete spectrum supplies the exact weights of the sharp cases of a blocking-pencil question, information not supplied by the much larger ambient rational-base histogram. The useful new data are those joint multiplicities, not the reproduction of the individual orbit or the aggregate count alone.
residual_risks: Finite, fixed-coordinate spectrum at q=3; no formula for larger fields or classification up to pencil isomorphism.
